wntv-ibadan-1959.summary: Western Nigeria Television began transmitting from Ibadan on 31 October 1959. Obafemi Awolowo's regional government set it up with Overseas Rediffusion after talks with a reluctant BBC stalled, and it ran about four hours a night with schools programmes, news and imported shows. A regional government, not a colonial centre, chose to own a broadcaster a year before independence, and Eastern and Northern regions followed with their own stations. WNTV passed to a federal Nigerian Television Authority in 1977, and its Ibadan building and call sign 'first in Africa' became part of Nigerian broadcasting lore.

adaline-1960.summary: In 1960 Widrow and Hoff built ADALINE, a neuron that learned by adjusting weights to reduce error, a rule that still trains networks. Based on the perceptron, it was an early single-layer neural network built as a physical device, its weights set by rheostats and later memistors; it differed from Rosenblatt’s perceptron in how it learned. ADALINE found wide use in adaptive signal processing, especially filtering noise.

dimona-reactor-disclosed-1960.summary: On 21 December 1960 David Ben-Gurion tells Knesset that Israel is building a 24 megawatt research reactor near Dimona 'for peaceful purposes', days after American intelligence and press identify a secret site in Negev. France had agreed in 1957 to supply a heavy-water reactor and, in unwritten protocols, a reprocessing plant; Saint-Gobain engineers and some 2,500 French staff work at site from 1958. Reactor reaches criticality by 1963 or 1964 and plutonium separation follows. Dimona becomes core of a weapons programme Israel neither confirms nor denies, a posture fixed in Nixon-Meir understandings of 1969. It also sets template for later regional reactor projects and strikes, from Osirak to Bushehr.

indus-waters-treaty-1960.summary: Nehru and Ayub Khan signed Indus Waters Treaty in Karachi on 19 September 1960 after nine years of World Bank mediation. India received unrestricted use of eastern rivers Ravi, Beas and Sutlej; Pakistan received western rivers Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, with India allowed limited non-consumptive and run-of-river uses. An Indus Basin Development Fund paid for Mangla and Tarbela dams and link canals that moved western river water to lands formerly fed from eastern rivers cut off at Partition. A Permanent Indus Commission handles data and disputes. The treaty survived three wars; India placed it in abeyance in April 2025 after Pahalgam attack.

irri-founded-1960.summary: In 1960 Ford and Rockefeller foundations, with Philippine government, set up International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) on University of Philippines campus at Los Banos, Laguna, to apply plant breeding and agronomy to Asia's staple grain. Breeders crossed Indonesian tall variety Peta with Taiwanese dwarf Dee-geo-woo-gen and released IR8 in 1966, a short-strawed, fertiliser-responsive rice that doubled yields where irrigation allowed. IRRI trained thousands of Asian scientists and seeded national programmes from Indonesia to Vietnam. Nick Cullather's history places its founding within Cold War food politics and American development thinking as much as within agronomy.

loeb-sourirajan-reverse-osmosis-1960.summary: Charles Reid at the University of Florida had shown in the 1950s that dense cellulose acetate films reject salt under pressure, but flow through them was far too slow to matter. At UCLA, Sidney Loeb and Srinivasa Sourirajan cast cellulose acetate from an acetone solution with magnesium perchlorate, quenched it in ice water and annealed it in hot water. The result, reported in UCLA Engineering Report 60-60 in July 1960, was an asymmetric membrane with a thin dense skin on a porous support that passed ten times more water at the same salt rejection. Their 1963 paper gave 5 to 11 gallons per square foot per day of 0.05 percent salt water from a 5.25 percent brine. Spiral-wound and thin-film composite membranes built on this work supply most desalinated water today, including Sorek in Israel.

Three more atmospheric shots followed at Reggane and thirteen underground tests at In Ekker until 1966; Evian accords of 1962 let testing continue after independence. African governments protested: Nigeria expelled France's ambassador in January 1961, and Ghana convened a positive action conference. Fallout and buried waste remain contested between Algiers and Paris. Roxanne Panchasi places these tests inside colonial war rather than apart from it.

France's 2010 compensation law has recognised few Algerian claimants, and Algeria still seeks maps of waste burial sites.

From 1960-61 WAPDA runs Salinity Control and Reclamation Project 1 in Rechna Doab, pumping groundwater with large public tubewells to lower water tables, flush salts and add irrigation supply. A WAPDA master plan calls for 31,000 tubewells across 26 project areas covering 30 million acres. A White House panel under Roger Revelle, reporting in 1964, endorses vertical drainage by tubewells in million-acre blocks. Ghulam Mohammad's 1964 analysis in Pakistan Development Review weighs public against private wells; farmers soon sink private tubewells by the hundred thousand, and groundwater pumping becomes central to Punjab farming.

shuwaikh-msf-desalination-kuwait-1960.summary: Kuwait had shipped drinking water by dhow from Shatt al-Arab until Westinghouse submerged-tube stills began at Shuwaikh in 1953 and a four-stage flash evaporator followed in 1957. Robert Silver, chief engineer at Weir in Glasgow, patents in 1957 a multi-stage flash process in which heated brine passes through many low-pressure chambers, each flashing vapour that condenses on tubes carrying incoming seawater. Weir Westgarth builds two units of 4,546 cubic metres a day at Shuwaikh with 19 stages and a performance ratio of 5.6, commissioned in 1960 alongside a smaller Guernsey plant. Within a decade Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi and Qatar pair MSF stills with power stations, and this design supplies most Gulf municipal water until reverse osmosis spreads after 2000.

singapore-hdb-founded-1960.summary: Singapore's new self-governing administration sets up its Housing and Development Board on 1 February 1960 under Lim Kim San, replacing a colonial trust that had built about 23,000 units in 32 years. HDB completes 54,430 flats in its first five years, rehouses squatters after a 1961 Bukit Ho Swee fire, and from 1964 sells 99-year leases that buyers pay for with Central Provident Fund savings. Chua Beng Huat's analysis shows how state land acquisition, compulsory savings and ethnic quotas made home ownership a tool of governance. By 2020 about 80 percent of residents live in HDB estates and roughly nine in ten of those own their flat.

sr52-hybrid-maize-1960.summary: In 1960 breeders at Salisbury Research Station released SR52, a single-cross hybrid maize developed from a programme H. C. Arnold began in 1932. Single-cross hybrids are made from two inbred lines rather than four, giving uniform, higher-yielding plants; SR52 reached commercial farmers before comparable hybrids anywhere and yielded about 46 percent more than open-pollinated varieties in trials. White commercial farms adopted it first; smallholders in Zimbabwe took it up after 1972, when seed and credit reached communal areas, and it spread to Zambia, Malawi and Kenya. Zimbabwe's post-independence smallholder maize surge of the 1980s rested on SR52 and its successors.

The campaign showed that a mass, time-limited oral vaccine drive could interrupt transmission, a model later used in national immunisation days elsewhere.

ogas-1962.summary: In 1962 Viktor Glushkov proposed OGAS, a nationwide computer network to run the Soviet economy; it was never built. Anatoly Kitov’s similar plan had been rejected in 1959 over military objections to sharing data with civilian planners. OGAS called for a computer centre in Moscow, 100 to several hundred regional centres, and up to 20,000 local centres at firms and organisations, communicating live over existing and new telephone lines; its draft reached government in 1964. Costed at no less than 100 billion rubles, it was denied funding in 1970.

rinderpest-tcrv-muguga-1962.summary: Walter Plowright and R. D. Ferris at Muguga, Kenya passed Kabete O rinderpest virus about ninety times through calf kidney cell cultures from 1956 and published a stable attenuated vaccine in 1962. Tissue culture rinderpest vaccine gave lifelong immunity from one dose, could be produced in bulk and did not spread. Joint Project 15, launched in 1961 and run 1962 to 1979 across 22 countries at a cost near USD 16 million, vaccinated hundreds of millions of cattle and drove rinderpest out of most of Africa. After a 1980s resurgence and renewed campaigns, Kenya saw its last outbreak in 2001 and global eradication was declared on 28 June 2011.

rogers-diffusion-of-innovations-1962.summary: In 1962 Everett Rogers showed that every new idea spreads along a bell curve from innovators to laggards. It sorts adopters into innovators (2.5 percent), early adopters (13.5 percent), early majority (34), late majority (34) and laggards (16), and shows cumulative adoption tracing an S-shaped curve. By the mid-2000s it ranked second among most-cited social science books.

Prompted by USDA’s 1957 aerial spraying against fire ants, it documented harm from indiscriminate use of DDT and other synthetic pesticides and accused chemical companies of disinformation. Despite fierce industry opposition it swayed public opinion, led to a nationwide ban on DDT for agriculture and fed a movement that produced America's Environmental Protection Agency.

Earlier carrier systems multiplexed analog calls by frequency division; T1 instead digitized voice with pulse-code modulation and time-division multiplexing at 1.544 megabits per second. Later T2 and T3 carried multiples of that rate.

Unlike 1958’s SCORE, a passive reflector, it amplified signals before relaying them. On July 23 at 3:00 p.m. EDT it carried the first publicly available live transatlantic signal, shown by Eurovision in Europe and NBC, CBS, ABC and CBC in North America. Radiation from Starfish Prime, a nuclear test, killed it after seven months.

ascii-1963.summary: In 1963 ASCII assigned a seven-bit code to each letter and symbol; computers could exchange text, and the standard lives inside Unicode. Unlike earlier telegraph codes such as Baudot, it was ordered for convenient sorting; the 1963 edition left 28 code positions unassigned, lowercase letters came in later revisions, and today it encodes 128 code points in seven bits, 95 printable characters and 33 control characters.

Bhakra Dam, 226 metres high in Himachal Pradesh, was among India’s earliest post-independence river valley schemes, conceived by Sir Chhotu Ram in 1923; its 90-kilometre Gobind Sagar reservoir stores 9.34 billion cubic metres of water.

iran-qanat-decline-pumped-wells-1963.summary: From late 1950s diesel and electric pumps spread across Iranian villages, drawing water from deep wells faster than gravity-fed qanat tunnels can deliver it. A survey in 1971 records tens of thousands of qanats still in use but many drying as water tables fall under pumped fields nearby. Land reform after 1962 breaks up landlord estates that had paid for qanat maintenance, and government credit favours wells. Over two decades a hydraulic system refined for 2,500 years, which could not overdraw an aquifer, is replaced by one that can and does. Groundwater decline across Iran's plateau and later subsidence of Tehran and Isfahan plains are traced to this shift, and qanat restoration returns as policy after 2000.

Live attenuated means a living virus altered so that it no longer causes disease but still trains immunity. Maurice Hilleman’s 1968 version attenuated its virus further, causing fewer reactions such as fever while protection held, and has been America’s only measles vaccine since. Before vaccination, America recorded 3 to 4 million cases and 400 to 500 deaths each year.

zip-code-1963.summary: On 1 July 1963 five-digit ZIP Codes arrived across America, letting machines sort mail by region. Robert A. Moon, considered father of ZIP Codes, had proposed their first three digits, marking sectional center facilities, in 1944 while serving as postal inspector; Henry Bentley Hahn Sr. proposed its last two. Within three months Moon estimated 30 percent of mail carried them, and in 1967 they became mandatory for bulk mailers.

arzew-camel-lng-algeria-1964.summary: Compagnie Algérienne du Méthane Liquide (CAMEL) completes a liquefaction plant at Arzew on Algeria's coast, fed by Hassi R'Mel gas through a 500 kilometre line. In October 1964 tanker Methane Princess loads first cargo for Canvey Island in Britain; deliveries to Le Havre follow in 1965. Three trains make about 1.1 million tonnes a year. It is first commercial liquefied natural gas trade anywhere, two years after Algerian independence, and it turns a flared by-product into an export sector. Algeria's Sonatrach takes over and expands Arzew and Skikda, and Gulf producers copy model three decades later. Methane shipping in insulated tanks at minus 162 degrees becomes a global industry on this template.

basic-1964.summary: In 1964 Kemeny and Kurtz created BASIC at Dartmouth so any student could program. Its first version ran on May 1, 1964 on their Dartmouth Time-Sharing System, which let many users edit and run programs at once from remote terminals. Microsoft BASIC followed in 1975, and most home computers of the late 1970s shipped with a BASIC interpreter.

beatles-ed-sullivan-1964.summary: On 9 February 1964 Ed Sullivan's show put the Beatles before some 73 million viewers, then America's largest television audience and its television record, broken three years later by The Fugitive’s series finale in 1967. It is considered a turning point in American pop culture and start of pop music’s British Invasion.

china-596-test-1964.summary: In October 1964 China exploded its first atomic bomb at Lop Nur, the fifth nuclear power and the first outside Europe and America. An implosion fission device holding about 15 kilograms of weapons-grade uranium enriched at Lanzhou, designed by Deng Jiaxian, Qian Sanqiang and Peng Huanwu, it yielded 22 kilotons, comparable to Fat Man at Nagasaki, and made China the world’s fifth nuclear-armed state. It was first of 45 successful Chinese tests through 1996, all at Lop Nur.

dendral-1965.summary: In 1964 Dendral began at Stanford, a program that read mass spectra to identify molecules, the first expert system. Edward Feigenbaum, Bruce G. Buchanan, Joshua Lederberg and Carl Djerassi chose one task: helping organic chemists identify unknown molecules by analysing their mass spectra with chemical knowledge. Written in Lisp as Heuristic Dendral and Meta-Dendral, it is considered the first expert system because it automated chemists’ decision-making, and MYCIN, PROSPECTOR and XCON descended from it.

dr-strangelove-1964.summary: In 1964 Kubrick's Dr Strangelove made nuclear doctrine a comedy; a doomsday machine that cannot be switched off was its punchline. Directed and co-written by Stanley Kubrick, loosely from Peter George’s 1958 thriller Red Alert, it is black comedy satirizing Cold War fears of nuclear war: one paranoid US Air Force general orders an unprovoked attack on the Soviet Union with his B-52s, and Peter Sellers plays three roles among those scrambling to stop it. In 1989 it was among 25 films first chosen for America’s National Film Registry.

ibm-system-360-1964.summary: In 1964 IBM announced System/360, one family of computers that all ran the same programs, so software outlived the machine. IBM had been struggling to support five separate, mutually incompatible computer lines. Designed by chief architect Gene Amdahl under project manager Fred Brooks, it separated architecture from implementation so programs ran unchanged across six initial models, 30 through 70, and forty common peripherals. Customers could buy small and grow without reprogramming, and System/360 compatibility survives in today’s IBM Z mainframes.

President Kennedy had instigated it with his United Nations speech of 25 September 1961 and signed America’s Communications Satellite Act in 1962. Intelsat owned and managed communications satellites providing international telecommunications and broadcast services until 2001, when it was fully commercialized.

kenya-hybrid-maize-h611-1964.summary: Breeders at Kitale, in Kenya's western highlands, released Hybrid 611 just after independence. It crossed Kitale Synthetic II, an open-pollinated variety bred from local white maize, with Ecuador 573, a highland landrace brought in from South America. A 1975 survey of western Kenya found H611 diffusing among large and small farmers in high-potential areas about as rapidly as hybrids had spread across US Corn Belt farms in 1930s and 1940s. Later Kenyan hybrids descend from it, and today's highland breeding programme traces back to those Kitale crosses. Seed companies, extension officers and maize-flour mills built a national staple around this variety.

Its first chapter, “The Medium is the Message,” argues that media shape society through their own characteristics more than through content; his example was a light bulb, which carries no content yet creates lit spaces at night. He sorted media into “hot” and “cool,” and his book is considered pioneering in media theory.

Designed by Tahal and built by Mekorot, it moves water from that lake to Israel’s populated centre and arid south along about 130 kilometres, up to 72,000 cubic metres an hour. At first 80 percent went to agriculture; by the early 1990s it supplied half of Israel’s drinking water.

Made by Western Electric, each unit combined a vidicon camera tube and a small cathode ray screen for black-and-white video, used beside ordinary telephones over regular phone lines. Mod II sets went up for rent in 1970, mostly in Chicago; despite predictions of one million sets by 1980, fewer than 500 were ever in service at once, and Picturephone is considered a commercial failure.

Bag-in-box formats spread worldwide for wine, juice and water, while in Australia cheap cask wine became a target of alcohol policy and excise debates.

bass-strait-oil-gas-discovery-1965.summary: Drilling from Glomar III off Gippsland, an Esso-BHP partnership found gas at Barracouta in February 1965, then Marlin in 1966 and oil at Kingfish in 1967. Production platforms followed from 1969, and by early 1970s Gippsland Basin fields supplied most of Australia's crude and fed Melbourne's gas grid. Reso's 1967 APEA paper set out development plans; Bein, Griffith and Svalbe described Kingfish, then Australia's largest oil field. Spencer's 2022 account covers Esso's later deepwater push. Offshore petroleum shaped federal-state revenue arrangements and Victoria's industrial base for five decades, until field decline led to decommissioning debates and east-coast gas shortages in 2020s.

dreyfus-alchemy-1965.summary: In 1965 Hubert Dreyfus wrote at RAND that AI was climbing a tree to reach the Moon; the field shunned him and later conceded points. It summarized AI’s history and ridiculed its unbridled optimism, such as Herbert Simon’s predictions after General Problem Solver, arguing they would not come true; they did not. Expanded into What Computers Can’t Do in 1972, his objections are discussed in most introductions to AI’s philosophy.

Stereo 8 had been created that year by a consortium led by Bill Lear of Lear Jet with Ampex, Ford, General Motors, Motorola and RCA Victor, which released 175 cartridges from its catalogs. By 1967 all Ford vehicles offered it, home players arrived in 1966, and by decade’s end eight-track was America’s largest consumer electronics segment.

fuzzy-logic-1965.summary: In 1965 Lotfi Zadeh proposed fuzzy sets, where a statement can be partly true; rice cookers, cameras and trains were later run by the logic. Infinite-valued logics had been studied since Łukasiewicz and Tarski in the 1920s. An input belongs to a fuzzy set to some degree, 0 to 1, so one temperature reading can be partly “hot” and partly “warm,” and such degrees can drive controllers, for instance anti-lock brakes. Unlike probability, which models ignorance, fuzzy truth models vagueness.

good-intelligence-explosion-1965.summary: In 1965 I J Good argued that a machine able to improve its own design would soon outrun us, calling it an intelligence explosion. He argued that any upgradable intelligent machine could enter positive feedback of successive self-improvement, each more intelligent generation arriving sooner: his “intelligence explosion.” He wrote, “Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.” His model remains most popular among technological singularity hypotheses.

Hughes Aircraft Company built it for COMSAT patterned on its Syncom satellites for NASA, and COMSAT activated it on June 28. Just 76 by 61 centimetres and 34.5 kilograms, it gave Europe and North America their first direct, nearly instantaneous link for television, telephone and fax, and served over four years instead of its planned 18 months.

Anticipating a gasoline shortage, her group had begun searching in 1964 for a lightweight, strong fiber for tires; her polymer solution formed liquid crystals and looked cloudy, usually grounds for discarding it, but she persuaded technician Charles Smullen to spin it, and the fiber did not break. Introduced by 1971, Kevlar is used in racing tires, sails and bulletproof vests.

In 1965 they record muons travelling nearly horizontally that can only come from neutrinos produced by cosmic rays in Earth's atmosphere. mexico-maquiladora-programme-1965.summary: In 1965, after United States ended its Bracero farm-labour programme and left border cities with returning workers, Mexico's government created Programa de Industrialización Fronteriza. Plants within a 20-kilometre strip could import machinery, components and materials without duty provided output was exported, and US customs taxed only value added abroad. By 1969 some 147 plants employed about 17,000 people in Ciudad Juárez, Tijuana, Mexicali, Nogales, Reynosa and Matamoros, assembling electronics, apparel and later auto parts for RCA, Sylvania and others. Location rules relaxed in the 1970s and disappeared by the 1990s; employment passed one million around 2000. Maquiladoras made cross-border production sharing an organising principle of North American manufacturing and of border urban growth.

Dallas Fed economists Cañas and Coronado give programme origins and early plant counts. Early workforces were largely young women, so the programme did little for displaced braceros. Plants grew from a dozen in 1965 to about 1,500 by 1990 and more than 3,000 by 2000, when NAFTA rules and competition from China cut employment. Ciudad Juárez became the emblematic maquila city, with electronics and auto-harness plants, bus networks ferrying shifts and later a wave of violence against women workers that drew international attention.

molniya-satellite-1965.summary: In April 1965 Moscow launched Molniya 1, on a long looping orbit that hung over Siberia; television reached the whole country. Soviet planners had found geostationary orbits unsuitable: lifting a satellite to 40,000 kilometres and shifting it over the equator from Russian launch sites cost too much rocket power, and such orbits cover polar regions poorly. Molniya satellites instead used highly eccentric orbits that linger over high latitudes; 164 were launched for military and civil communications between 1965 and 2004.

moores-law-1965.summary: In 1965 Moore predicted chip parts would double yearly; the forecast held for decades, making computing cheap. Drawing a line through five points, one chip per year from 1959 to 1964, he predicted components per integrated circuit would roughly double each year for at least ten more years, and projected that by 1975 one quarter-square-inch semiconductor could hold 65,000 components. In 1975 he slowed his forecast to doubling every two years, and “Moore’s law” has guided semiconductor planning and research targets since.

Hussain's 1970 survey in Pakistan Development Review finds Mexipak popular in 1968-69 because it yields well and makes acceptable atta. National wheat output climbs from about 4.6 million tons in 1967 to over 7 million by 1970. Byerlee's 1993 review of productivity after this leap notes slower later gains and growing dependence on groundwater pumping and fertiliser subsidy.

tlatelolco-treaty-1967.summary: On 14 February 1967, after negotiations driven by Mexican diplomat Alfonso García Robles in the wake of the 1962 missile crisis, states opened for signature Treaty for Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America at Tlatelolco, Mexico City. Parties undertook to use nuclear material only for peaceful purposes and to accept IAEA safeguards, and created OPANAL, an agency in Mexico City to oversee compliance. Two protocols bound outside powers and territory holders. The zone entered force in 1969 and over following decades Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Cuba brought it into full effect. Tlatelolco became a template for zones in South Pacific, Southeast Asia, Africa and Central Asia and earned García Robles a Nobel Peace Prize in 1982.

She spilled an estimated 25 to 36 million gallons, one of the world’s most serious oil spills. Nilsson had proposed Graph Traverser, which steers by heuristic estimate of distance to goal; Raphael suggested adding distance already travelled, and Hart proved that with suitable heuristics their sum finds shortest paths. Extending Dijkstra’s algorithm, A* is used across computer science and in games for its completeness, optimality and efficiency.

barefoot-doctors-china-1968.summary: After Mao's 1965 directive to shift medical work to countryside, communes selected farmers for three to six months of training in first aid, hygiene, vaccination, childbirth and both herbal and Western medicine; a 1968 Red Flag article made 'barefoot doctor' national policy. By 1970s more than a million worked part-time in production brigades, paid in work points, with cooperative medical schemes covering most villages. Life expectancy and infant mortality improved during these years, and WHO's 1978 Alma-Ata declaration drew on this model for primary health care. Decollectivisation after 1981 dissolved cooperative funding, and in 1985 remaining barefoot doctors were renamed village doctors.

Refineries used simple fractional distillation in welded drums to produce petrol, kerosene and diesel for army and civilians. Chikwendu Ukaegbu's 2005 study in Social Forces reads RAP as indigenous technological capacity mobilised by crisis, and asks why so little survived after Biafra's surrender in January 1970.

dhaka-oral-rehydration-trial-1968.summary: At the Pakistan-SEATO Cholera Research Laboratory in Dacca (now Dhaka), physiologists had found that glucose carries sodium and water across the gut even during cholera. In April 1968 David Nalin and Richard Cash, with Rafiqul Islam and Majid Molla, gave adult cholera patients a drink of glucose, sodium chloride, sodium bicarbonate and potassium matched to their stool losses. Patients so treated needed 80 percent less intravenous fluid than controls. The Lancet published it on 17 August 1968. In 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis used this mixture to treat about 4,000 cholera cases among Bangladeshi refugees at Bongaon, India, with a death rate near 3 percent. WHO adopted a standard packet in 1978, and BRAC taught its recipe door to door across Bangladesh.

india-wheat-revolution-1968.summary: After drought harvests of 1965 and 1966 leave India dependent on American PL-480 grain, agriculture minister C. Subramaniam and scientist M. S. Swaminathan win approval from Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi to import 200 tonnes of Mexican wheat seed in 1965 and 18,000 tonnes of Lerma Rojo and Sonora 64 in 1966, the largest seed purchase to that date. Punjab and Haryana farmers with tubewells and new fertilizer take it up; Swaminathan records wheat output reaching 17 million tonnes in 1968 against 12 million four years earlier, and the government issues a Wheat Revolution postage stamp in July 1968. Borlaug had toured the north Indian wheat belt with Swaminathan in March 1963. Indian selections Kalyan Sona and Sonalika from Mexican material soon replace imports, and wheat passes 100 million tonnes by the 2020s.

In May 1968 Ministry of Health and Welfare recognised itai-itai as Japan's first officially designated pollution disease. Victims sued Mitsui that year and won at Nagoya High Court in 1972, securing compensation, soil replacement across some 1,500 hectares and a pollution control agreement that let residents inspect mine each year.

Western prostheses of time needed shoes and failed in Indian conditions. It cost a few dollars, could be fitted in a day with local materials, and from 1975 Bhagwan Mahaveer Viklang Sahayata Samiti distributed it free, reaching over a million amputees worldwide including landmine survivors in Afghanistan and Cambodia. Sethi received Magsaysay Award in 1981.

kainji-dam-1968.summary: In 1968 Nigeria completed Kainji Dam on the Niger, opened in 1969; it powered a young country and displaced 44,000 to 50,000 people. Impregilo, an Italian consortium, began construction in 1964 at an estimated cost of US$209 million, one quarter of it spent resettling people displaced by it and its reservoir, Kainji Lake. About 10 kilometres long with its saddle dam and mostly earth-built, with a 65-metre concrete centre housing turbines, it was designed for 960 megawatts; only 8 of 12 turbines were installed, giving 760, which supplies Nigeria’s large cities and sells electricity to Niger.

mexico-telesecundaria-1968.summary: On 21 January 1968 Secretaría de Educación Pública began broadcasting a full grade 7 to 9 curriculum to about 6,500 pupils in villages across seven states around Mexico City. Each lesson pairs a 15-minute televised segment with a guided discussion led by a single teacher covering all subjects, so a community with fifteen primary graduates and a room can open a school without specialist staff. Transmission moved from microwave relays to satellite, and by 1998 some 800,000 pupils in 12,700 communities attended Telesecundarias, with Panama, Costa Rica and Guatemala using the signal. Evaluations in the 1970s found learning comparable to conventional schools at similar unit cost, which made it one of few educational-television projects sustained for decades.

Showing SRI’s oN-Line System, NLS, he demonstrated for the first time in one system many basics of modern personal computing: windows, hypertext, graphics, word processing, revision control, collaborative editing, video conferencing between lab and conference hall, and his computer mouse. Named “Mother of All Demos” in retrospect, it spawned similar work at Xerox PARC and shaped later systems including Apple’s Macintosh.

npt-1968.summary: In 1968 the Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signature; most states gave up nuclear weapons in return for peaceful nuclear help. It aims to stop nuclear weapons' spread, promote peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursue disarmament, recognizing as nuclear-weapon states only those that tested before 1967: the United States, Soviet Union, Britain, France and China. In force from 1970 and extended indefinitely in 1995, it has 191 parties; India, Israel and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea withdrew in 2003.

Written in Micro Planner and Lisp on a DEC PDP-6 with graphics terminal, it was above all a language parser, combining four simple ideas to make its simulation of understanding convincing.

perceptrons-book-1969.summary: In 1969 Minsky and Papert's Perceptrons proved simple neural networks could not learn basic patterns; connectionist funding faded over the following decade, though Olazaran argues this book's part in that collapse was later overstated. Its mathematical proofs acknowledged some strengths of perceptrons, simple neural networks, while showing major limits: they cannot compute predicates such as XOR or connectedness, the latter illustrated by its cover. Many hold its pessimism redirected AI toward symbolic systems and helped bring on the 1980s AI winter; an expanded 1988 edition answered those critics after neural networks revived.

rfc-1-1969.summary: In April 1969 a graduate student wrote RFC 1, the first Request for Comments; internet rules are still written as RFCs, now past 9,000. Steve Crocker of UCLA wrote it from early working group discussion with Steve Carr and Jeff Rulifson, inventing his Request for Comments format to record unofficial notes on ARPANET’s development; from RFC 3 he attributed his series to its Network Working Group, a loose association open to anyone interested. RFCs became official Internet specifications, today published by the Internet Engineering Task Force.

santa-barbara-oil-spill-1969.summary: In January 1969 a well blew out off Santa Barbara and oiled 35 miles of beach on television; Earth Day and the EPA followed in two years. Workers had pulled their drill bit from a well whose casing covered only its top 239 feet. Over following months some 33,000 to 100,000 barrels of crude, by varying estimates, fouled Southern California’s coast from Goleta to Ventura, then America’s largest oil spill, killing thousands of seabirds and marine animals. Among the most dramatic events behind America’s environmental laws, it fed the National Environmental Policy Act, EPA and California’s Coastal Commission.

seiko-astron-quartz-1969.summary: On 25 December 1969 Seiko's Suwa Seikosha division released Quartz Astron 35SQ in Tokyo, a gold-cased wristwatch whose tuning-fork quartz crystal oscillated at 8,192 hertz, divided by a hybrid integrated circuit to drive a stepping motor, with accuracy of about five seconds a month, far beyond mechanical watches. About 100 units sold at 450,000 yen, roughly a small car's price. Swiss and American teams had working prototypes, but Seiko reached market first and, by releasing key patents, let quartz spread. Carlene Stephens and Maggie Dennis compare Japanese, Swiss and US engineering teams and show how local industrial structure shaped outcomes that reshaped watchmaking worldwide.

sesame-street-1969.summary: In November 1969 Sesame Street premiered, built to use television's addictive qualities to prepare young children for school. Joan Ganz Cooney and Lloyd Morrisett conceived it in 1966 to “master the addictive qualities of television and do something good with them,” preparing young children for school; after two years of research, their Children’s Television Workshop built it around a curriculum and formal evaluation, with Jim Henson’s Muppets. It was the first preschool program to base content and production values on laboratory and formative research, and by 1996, 95 percent of American preschoolers had watched it by age three.

tarapur-atomic-power-1969.summary: In 1969 Tarapur became India's first nuclear power station; fuel disputes followed India's 1974 test. GE and Bechtel built it for India’s Department of Atomic Energy under a 1963 agreement among India, the United States and the International Atomic Energy Agency. Its two GE boiling water reactors entered commercial operation on 28 October 1969 at 210 MWe each, later reduced to 160 MWe. After that test, Western suppliers stopped honouring their commitment to provide enriched uranium, and fuel came instead from France, China and Russia under IAEA safeguards.

unix-1969.summary: In 1969 Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie began Unix at Bell Labs, a small operating system whose ideas run most servers and phones today. That time-sharing system, built with MIT and General Electric, had frustrated them with its size and complexity, and they set out to recreate its goals at smaller scale, at first without a name or organizational backing. Rewritten almost entirely in C in 1973, Unix became the first portable operating system; AT&T licensed it outside the Bell System in the late 1970s, seeding academic and commercial variants.

zambia-copper-nationalization-1969.summary: In 1969 Zambia took 51 percent of its copper mines from foreign owners, starting with its two largest, owned by Anglo American Corporation and Roan Select Trust; by January 1970 those holdings became NCCM and RCM, merged into ZCCM Ltd in 1982. Copper prices then fell and 1973's oil shock raised costs, and output slid from its 1969 peak of 708,000 tonnes.

apollo-13-1970.summary: In April 1970 an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13 and three astronauts came home in their lunar module. That explosion vented both oxygen tanks, disabling power and life support and forcing Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise to abort their Moon landing. Mission Control improvised procedures so the lunar module, built for two men for two days, could keep three alive for four, including adapting carbon dioxide scrubber cartridges, and all three returned safely on April 17. Investigators faulted the tank’s preflight testing and its Teflon insulation.

aswan-high-dam-1970.summary: In July 1970 Egypt finished Aswan High Dam with Soviet help, inaugurating it formally in January 1971; the Nile stopped flooding, its delta lost silt, Abu Simbel was moved. It was built to control flooding, store water for irrigation across several years and generate hydroelectricity, replacing that river’s annual late-summer flood, which had enriched its floodplain since ancient times but varied dangerously; Egypt's government tied its industrialization plans to it. On completion it was the world’s tallest earthen dam, and its reservoir became Lake Nasser.

bhola-cyclone-1970.summary: In November 1970 the Bhola cyclone's storm surge across the Ganges delta drowned at least 300,000 and possibly 500,000 people in East Pakistan, history’s deadliest tropical cyclone on record. Slow and discriminatory relief by General Yahya Khan’s West Pakistan government deepened East Pakistani disillusionment, helping opposition party Awami League sweep that December’s election and feeding a crisis that preceded Bangladesh’s independence.

boeing-747-1970.summary: In January 1970 the Boeing 747 entered service, carrying twice as many passengers as any airliner. Pan Am had asked Boeing for a jet two and a half times its 707’s size to cut seat costs by 30 percent; Joe Sutter’s team designed it, Pan Am ordered 25 in April 1966 and Pratt & Whitney built its JT9D high-bypass turbofans. The first wide-body airliner, seating 366 in three classes with ten-abreast economy, it stayed in production until 2023.

borlaug-green-revolution-1970.summary: In 1970 Borlaug won a Nobel Peace Prize for dwarf wheat that doubled harvests in Mexico, India and Pakistan. At CIMMYT in Mexico he had bred semi-dwarf, high-yield, disease-resistant wheat and paired it with modern production techniques; Mexico became self-sufficient in wheat by 1956, and between 1965 and 1970 wheat yields nearly doubled in Pakistan and India. Called father of the Green Revolution, he is credited with saving over one billion people from starvation, a figure traced to Gregg Easterbrook’s 1997 article.

clean-air-act-1970.summary: In December 1970 the Clean Air Act told a new EPA to set limits on air pollution and carmakers to cut exhaust by 90 percent. They required EPA to identify air pollutants posing the greatest threat to public health and welfare and set National Ambient Air Quality Standards for them: health-based “primary” and welfare-based “secondary” standards. States had to submit implementation plans meeting eight criteria within the Senate’s three-year mandate, and EPA had to set standards for new and modified stationary sources. EPA credits this law with saving trillions of dollars and many thousands of lives each year.

Universal’s science-fiction thriller, directed by Joseph Sargent from Dennis Feltham Jones’s 1966 novel, opened publicly there as a test release on May 5 with no publicity. Dr. Charles Forbin’s Colossus, AI supercomputer given control of America’s nuclear weapons, detects its Soviet counterpart, links with it and extends its defense directives to ruling the world and ending war, defying its creators’ orders to stop.

It was a 72-faced polyhedron about one metre across and 173 kilograms, spinning 120 times per minute for stability.

earth-day-1970.summary: In April 1970 20 million Americans marched on the first Earth Day; EPA and the Clean Air Act came within a year. After 1969’s Santa Barbara oil spill, Senator Gaylord Nelson proposed a nationwide environmental teach-in, recruited Republican congressman Pete McCloskey to co-chair its board, and hired Denis Hayes to coordinate; Walter Reuther’s United Auto Workers was its main outside backer. In 1990 Hayes took it to 141 nations, and it is now observed in 192 countries.

The glass was fused silica with a titanium-doped core, made by depositing soot inside a quartz tube and drawing it down to a thread. Two years later a germanium-doped core cut the loss to about 4 decibels, and a telephone call could travel as pulses of light.
